We demonstrate the generation of an optical frequency comb within a microtoroidal resonator using a low-frequency (100 Hz) parametric modulation applied to the cavity's drive. This technique effectively "plants" comb lines at specific intervals determined by the modulation frequency, with the resulting spectrum exhibiting a high degree of regularity. The study further explores the influence of modulation depth and frequency on the spectral spacing and power levels of these planted lines.

This study examines the properties of the space of isometric actions on real trees that are invariant under random subgroup selections within groups exhibiting acylindrical hyperbolicity. We demonstrate that for any such group, these properties form a locally compact, Polish space equipped with a unique minimal $G$-invariant probability measure, representing a Loyal Random Subgroup. Furthermore, we establish that the collection of these Loyal Random Subgroups forms a closed $G$-subshift within the broader space of all such actions.

We investigate the behavior of overparameterized binary neural networks trained via stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on linearly separable tasks. Our findings indicate that as training progresses, the network's weight distributions converge to binary states, causing the training error to asymptotically approach zero. Furthermore, by employing the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) framework, we establish that the NTK itself converges to a binary distribution during training. Leveraging this insight, we derive an upper bound for the generalization error, demonstrating that the binary weight architecture facilitates superior generalization performance.

We introduce a new class of surfaces, termed the "extremal surface," which generalizes the concept of quantum extremal surfaces. These surfaces arise as the critical points of the entanglement entropy functional for a specific subsystem, selected from all possible extremal surfaces. We demonstrate that this category encompasses both the standard extremal surfaces associated with entanglement entropy and the island surfaces responsible for black hole evaporation. Additionally, we outline an iterative algorithm capable of locating these surfaces and prove their uniqueness under particular conditions. Applying this framework, we derive a set of universal inequalities governing entanglement entropy within a broad range of holographic systems, referred to as the "holographic entropy prism." These results extend the Reeb's second law of thermodynamics and the strong subadditivity principle to more general contexts.

We introduce a crossing factor $K$ that commutes with all members of the transfer matrices for the solvable lattice models studied in this paper. This factor establishes an equivalence between two interlinked sets of these matrices, thereby proving the Yang-Baxter equation.

This study introduces and examines the stabilization techniques applied to the iterative Nesterov–FISTA algorithm used for solving convex inverse problems. We demonstrate that applying these methods yields a new class of convergent algorithms, with their performance validated through numerical tests on compressed sensing tasks.

This study examines the point spread functions (PSFs) of composite images created by merging multiple exposures with varying PSFs, a standard procedure in contemporary astronomical imaging. We demonstrate that the PSF of a co-added image is not a simple average of the individual component PSFs. Instead, it represents a weighted mean where weights depend on the signal-to-noise ratio of each exposure. Furthermore, we derive an analytical estimate for the co-added image's effective full width at half maximum (FWHM) and validate these findings through Monte Carlo simulations.

We introduce a framework for Gaussian free fields (GFfs) on the unit disk that integrate with systems of multiple Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) curves. This model applies specifically when the curves' driving functions constitute log-gas configurations influenced by log-gases.

This paper establishes the $L^p$-norm bounds for the pressure and derives corresponding estimates for the velocity field of the Navier-Stokes equations, expressed via the maximum norm of the Biot-Savart kernel. Leveraging these $L^p$-pressure estimates, the study derives conditions for the global existence and boundedness of smooth solutions to the periodic Navier-Stokes equations.

Quantum computing offers a promising avenue for solving specific problems more efficiently than classical methods. However, the inherent susceptibility of quantum systems to noise poses a significant obstacle to their practical application. To address this, Mahadev introduced a groundbreaking protocol that enables a classical verifier to confirm the accuracy of a quantum computation using only minimal quantum resources. While theoretically sound, this method relies on cryptographic assumptions and incurs excessive classical and quantum resource costs, rendering it impractical for large-scale scenarios. In this work, we present an enhanced version of Mahadev's framework that maintains the low-quantum-memory advantage but drastically cuts down classical time complexity. Our method achieves this by leveraging succinct arguments for NP, thereby accelerating verification to linear time relative to the input size.

This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to model the morphological dynamics of animal cells. By representing cellular structures as implicit surfaces, the model utilizes a neural network to map spatial coordinates to signed distance values. The network is trained using a variational approach to generate novel cell shapes, with the learning process guided by a loss function that combines a data-driven prior on shape and a smoothness prior on the latent space. The proposed approach is validated using a dataset of interphase HeLa cells, demonstrating its ability to accurately model shape evolution.

This work examines how reinforcement learning can be applied to develop space representations in autonomous agents, utilizing a modular approach that trains a predictive head alongside a primary policy network. We evaluate this framework across three distinct tasks: a spatial navigation task, a foraging task, and a hierarchical navigation task. Results indicate that the proposed method effectively learns representations capable of supporting these activities. Furthermore, we assess the generalization capabilities of the acquired representations by testing them in novel environments and with altered sensor inputs.

This study introduces a hard-disk dipole system featuring long-range repulsive forces, wherein the hard-disk nature prevents any two particles from occupying the same space. The system's dynamics are governed by a non-reversible Markov process that combines continuous movement with discrete jumps. The continuous phase follows a Gibbs measure determined by an external field, while the discrete jumps operate under a specific, non-reversible protocol. The research focuses on the system's hydrodynamic behavior, deriving both the macroscopic balance equation and the corresponding current. The analysis reveals that the macroscopic measure differs from the microscopic one, indicating that the dynamics are non-symmetrizable. Furthermore, the derived macroscopic currents demonstrate non-linearity and non-conservation, highlighting the significant impact of the non-symmetrizable jump component on the system's behavior.

Sound event localization and identification (SELID) is a critical field within audio processing, aiming to detect active sound sources and determine their positions. This paper introduces a novel SELID framework that employs Convolutional Recurrent Neural Networks (CRNN) to process microphone array data. The system utilizes a 2D convolutional layer with rectangular filters to extract features from the input spectrograms. To enhance the model's robustness, the training data undergoes data augmentation through channel rotation. The network is trained to predict the probability of specific sound classes alongside their directional estimates. Experimental results indicate that this approach achieves superior performance in SELID tasks compared to existing methods.

Concurrent transmission (CT) within wireless networks enables multiple users to transmit data simultaneously across the same frequency spectrum, thereby enhancing spectral efficiency. This paper offers a comprehensive survey of contemporary research on wireless systems leveraging CT, covering the following key areas: (1) an overview of the primary techniques used to facilitate CT, including non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), interference alignment (IA), and analog network coding (ANC); (2) a detailed analysis of the most prevalent multiple-antenna approaches, such as successive interference cancellation (SIC), linear and non-linear receivers, and dirty paper coding (DPC); (3) a review of the most common performance metrics, specifically focusing on outage probability, ergodic capacity, and error probability; and (4) a summary of the most significant open challenges in the field.

This study introduces a novel time-frequency (TF) analysis framework grounded in stochastic geometry. The approach models a TF signal as a Poisson point process, treating the signal's spectrogram level sets as the boundaries of a corresponding random closed set. By leveraging this framework, the authors derive a novel estimator for the signal's energy. Simulation results demonstrate that this estimator exhibits strong performance, maintaining robustness even in the presence of significant noise.

Chimeras are dynamical states characterized by the coexistence of synchronized groups and travelling waves, a phenomenon observed across various physical systems. This study introduces a robust methodology for detecting these waves and synchronized clusters within spiking networks, grounded in the analysis of travelling wave properties and the clustering of spatio-temporal firing patterns. The proposed technique is validated through its application to a model featuring a ring of coupled excitatory neurons with localized inhibition and travelling wave drivers. The results demonstrate that the method effectively identifies wave fronts and clusters, even in the presence of significant noise and heterogeneity.

This study introduces a new module for REBOUND, a widely used N-body simulation package, designed to apply the Ito interpretation of the Langevin equation. This module enables researchers to model systems influenced by random effects, such as those caused by unresolved small bodies or gas, as well as to conduct simulations under conditions of constant energy or volume. The module is highly versatile, allowing users to define various noise profiles, including Gaussian and colored noise, and to choose between different stochastic integration techniques.

We introduce a quantum Fokker-Planck operator equation designed to describe the stochastic dynamics of continuously measured and feedback-controlled open quantum systems. This framework incorporates both measurement-induced back-action and the influence of linear feedback loops. By utilizing this operator formalism, we demonstrate that specific stochastic trajectories can steer a system into a pure state, effectively achieving measurement-based quantum state preparation.

We examine a one-dimensional confinement where disks of two distinct radii, $r_1$ and $r_2$, are randomly packed. The system's weight is determined by the count of disks of the second type. The study focuses on the system's weight distribution, the frequency of sequences with identical consecutive disk types, and the mean length of these sequences. The analysis covers the system's behavior under varying ratios of the two disk radii and disk counts, supported by both numerical simulations and theoretical modeling.

The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a dominant driver of global climate variability, yet its impacts on extreme precipitation events remain complex and difficult to decipher. This study investigates the distinct signatures of canonical and Modoki ENSO events within global seasonal extremes of both high and low precipitation. Utilizing a 1950–2019 ERA5 reanalysis dataset, we identified significant differences in the spatial distribution of these extremes between the two ENSO flavors. Specifically, canonical ENSO events exhibit a broader influence on seasonal precipitation extremes compared to Modoki events. Furthermore, the study reveals that the seasonal cycle of extreme precipitation extremes is modulated differently by canonical and Modoki ENSO events, with the magnitude of this modulation varying across different regions. These findings underscore the necessity of distinguishing between unique ENSO flavors when analyzing ENSO-related impacts on global precipitation extremes.

The identification of massive black hole (BH) progenitors is essential for understanding the growth of supermassive black holes (SMBHs). We examine observational indicators of these progenitors in dwarf galaxies, specifically focusing on the Leo I system. Our analysis reveals that Leo I exhibits a high specific star formation rate (sSFR) alongside a low specific BH surface density (SBH), suggesting the presence of a massive BH progenitor. We evaluate two primary formation channels: the collapse of massive stars within dense star clusters and the merger of smaller black holes in globular clusters. Our findings indicate that the BH surface density in Leo I is insufficient to account for the observed SBH solely through the initial collapse of stars in dense clusters. Conversely, the merger of black holes within globular clusters offers a viable explanation for the observed SBH. Consequently, Leo I likely hosts a massive BH progenitor formed via globular cluster mergers, providing significant insights into the early development of supermassive black holes.

Multi-orbital kagome materials are renowned for their flat band structures, which facilitate strong electron correlations and exotic quantum phenomena. This study investigates the magnetotransport characteristics of Bi$_3$Ir$_2$Sn$_2$O$_{12}$, a multi-orbital kagome alloy, revealing that its transport behavior is governed by the flat band. We observe a pronounced negative magnetoresistance (MR) at low temperatures, which is attributed to the suppression of weak localization via a magnetic field. Furthermore, the field dependence of resistance aligns with the scaling laws of the quantum Hall effect, suggesting that the MR originates from the suppression of inter-orbital scattering due to the magnetic field. Additionally, the resistance displays a linear relationship with temperature, a signature of the Aharonov-Bohm effect. These findings indicate that multi-orbital kagome compounds offer a promising avenue for exploring novel quantum states arising from flat band physics.

Genomic functional data and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) offer complementary insights into the genetic underpinnings of complex traits. This study integrates functional annotations with GWAS results for 18 human traits to identify trait-specific functional elements and genes. We detected significant enrichment of GWAS signals within regulatory regions, including promoters, transcription factor binding sites, and RNA polymerase II occupancy zones. Furthermore, we identified 1,000 genomic regions exhibiting strong, trait-specific enrichment, with many containing genes linked to those traits. Finally, we developed a method to pinpoint genes with the highest probability of involvement in a trait by aggregating evidence from functional enrichment and GWAS data.

This paper investigates block arrangements where each block contains exactly $r$ points, with every pair of points co-occurring in $\lambda$ blocks. We demonstrate that if the greatest common divisor of $r$ and $\lambda$ equals one, then such an arrangement cannot possess a flag-transitive automorphism group unless the structure degenerates into a symmetric block design.

This study examines the one-dimensional confined helium atom, utilizing information entropy criteria alongside correlation information potentials to evaluate electron-electron correlation effects. We employ a flexible trial wave function featuring adjustable parameters for both single-particle and two-body terms. Results indicate that incorporating a two-body term significantly enhances the wave function's quality, as evidenced by reduced values for both information entropies and correlation information potentials.

The wide binary test investigates the large-scale behavior of gravity by examining the orbital dynamics of widely separated binary stars. This study introduces a novel perspective on the test by employing a new set of variables that are invariant under Galilean transformations, thereby eliminating the need to specify a specific reference frame. We demonstrate that these variables adhere to Newtonian equations of motion and can be integrated analytically. Furthermore, we show that the variable representing the binary's position relative to the system's barycenter functions as an adiabatic parameter, allowing the equations to be reduced to a two-dimensional phase space. Finally, we outline the strategy for implementing the test and address the associated uncertainties.

This work investigates the removal of logical rules within multiplicative linear logic, specifically addressing both exponential-free systems and those incorporating Parigot's modalities. We demonstrate that, in the presence of cut elimination, any proof containing only multiplicative rules constitutes a constructive proof of the underlying statement. Consequently, such proofs yield normal forms that are free of cuts.

This study introduces a novel methodology for forecasting the synchronization state of financial time series, with the ultimate goal of anticipating the synchronization breakdown that often precedes market crashes. The proposed approach leverages cross-recurrence plots to quantify the degree of synchronization between two time series, while a machine learning model is employed to predict the subsequent evolution of these synchronization metrics. The research utilizes historical data from the S&P 500 and the FTSE 100 indices, covering the period from 1990 to 2017.

We introduce a theoretical framework for modeling electron-phonon coupling that explicitly accounts for the momentum dependence of both electron and phonon properties. This approach yields analytical expressions for the electron-phonon and electron-electron interaction matrices, as well as the renormalized phonon self-energy. We demonstrate that including electron and phonon momentum variations can induce novel interactions, such as generating a finite electron-phonon coupling strength even in systems where it would otherwise be zero. Furthermore, we show that these momentum effects can significantly alter the magnitude of the electron-phonon interaction and modify the nature of the resulting renormalized phenomena.

In the realm of online advertising, click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a critical component for ad ranking and charging strategies. However, the introduction of new advertisements presents significant challenges, primarily due to the scarcity of historical data and the difficulty of estimating user preferences. This study proposes a novel approach that leverages visual content to bolster CTR predictions for these fresh ads. Specifically, we design a dual-stage framework: initially, a multi-task learning model extracts features from ad images to forecast CTR, and subsequently, these refined features are integrated into the primary CTR prediction system. Empirical evaluations on a real-world advertising dataset demonstrate that our method yields substantial performance gains.

Business Process Management (BPM) has become a vital domain for modeling and executing workflows within organizations. Among various BPMN constructs, case models are particularly significant for representing process instances. This paper introduces a method for enriching case models with cardinality constraints to limit the number of times specific activities occur within an instance. We present an algorithm capable of verifying constraint satisfaction within a given case model and provide a mechanism for transforming constraint violations into new, refined constraints. Furthermore, we have developed a prototype implementation to validate our approach.

This study introduces a physics-informed statistical model designed to forecast wildfire aerosols by integrating remote-sensing data with numerical models. The proposed methodology combines a statistical framework for estimating cloud-top heights of pyrocumulus clouds with a numerical model that simulates aerosol transport and dispersion. The statistical component utilizes a deep learning algorithm to analyze infrared and water vapor channels from geostationary satellites, specifically targeting pyrocumulus cloud detection and height estimation. These estimated heights then serve as initial conditions for the numerical model, which calculates the subsequent evolution of the aerosol plume. The system's performance was evaluated using data from the GOES-16 satellite alongside the HYSPLIT numerical model. Results indicate that this hybrid approach achieves superior accuracy in predicting aerosol concentrations compared to standard simulations that rely solely on conventional cloud-top height inputs.

We introduce a new privacy framework for GPS data known as Conditional Location Privacy (CLP). This model defines a mechanism that generates a privacy-preserving trajectory from an original one, ensuring the obscured path remains close to the true route while maintaining the original's semantic integrity. A mechanism satisfies CLP if the resulting trajectory adheres to a specific conditional distribution determined by the adversary's prior beliefs. We propose a novel prior distribution that captures the inherent characteristics of real-world movement patterns, which in turn yields mechanisms offering superior semantic fidelity. Additionally, we present an efficient algorithm for constructing these CLP mechanisms and provide empirical evidence demonstrating their performance.

This study investigates multisite resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data to evaluate the reliability and predictive validity of connectivity estimates. We demonstrate that, although signal-to-noise ratios are generally low, the strength of the underlying signals and their accuracy improve significantly with longer scan durations. Furthermore, we show that the predictive validity of these connectivity estimates is highly dependent on the specific brain regions examined.

Building upon the work of Lott-Villani and Sturm, we present a definition of Ricci curvature for metric measure graphs that aligns with the broader framework of $\text{RCCMS}(K,\infty)$ spaces. Within this definition, we prove a concentration of measure theorem and demonstrate that it implies a Leonard-type inequality associated with $\text{RCCMS}(K,\infty)$ spaces. Furthermore, we establish a Poincaré inequality and prove an equivalent characterization of $\text{RCCMS}(K,\infty)$ spaces involving a $\text{LCCMS}(K,\infty)$-type gradient estimate for a Markov semigroup.

Code-mixed language, which involves interleaving two or more languages, is prevalent in numerous parts of the globe. Although recent research has largely concentrated on NLP tasks for such languages, a significant hurdle remains: the scarcity of annotated datasets. To address this, this study introduces PESTO, a novel position encoding technique designed to enhance the performance of pre-trained language models (PLMs) on code-mixed data. PESTO functions by utilizing a switching mechanism that adapts the positional embeddings of a PLM based on the specific language identified at each token. Empirical evaluations across multiple tasks and datasets demonstrate that PESTO consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the electron-phonon coupling and the isotope effect in H$_3$S under varying pressures. Our results indicate that the isotope effect coefficient ($\alpha$) rises with increasing pressure, reaching a maximum of 0.52 at 200 GPa. Additionally, the calculated electron-phonon coupling constant ($\lambda$) exhibits a slight decline as pressure increases. The observed increase in $\alpha$ is primarily driven by the van Hove singularity in the electronic density of states, which intensifies with pressure. The calculated critical temperature ($T_c$) aligns well with experimental data, showing a peak of 206 K at 200 GPa. The study concludes that the pressure-induced shift in the phonon spectrum and the van Hove singularity in the density of states are the key factors responsible for the maximum $T_c$ observed at 200 GPa.

Fisher's average effect is a fundamental concept in statistical genetics, serving as a cornerstone for quantitative genetics. This study demonstrates that this metric possesses causal relevance, specifically representing the causal impact of a gene on a phenotype under the assumption of a binary gene model. By linking Fisher's average effect to the concept of natural selection, the work provides a novel perspective on statistical genetics.

This paper introduces a thruster-supported locomotion framework designed to improve the efficiency and robustness of legged robots. The proposed method relies on a simplified model of the robot's dynamics, which is solved using a sampling-based optimal control technique. This approach determines both the robot's gait and the necessary thrusts to execute it. The resulting control policy is then applied to a full dynamic simulation to validate the method. The study concludes with a demonstration of the generated control strategies, showcasing their ability to handle disturbances and adapt to uneven surfaces.

This study introduces a novel visual relocalization approach that leverages 3D surfel maps. The method employs a learned descriptor for initial viewpoint selection and subsequently refines the camera pose through an optimization process. To enhance robustness, the descriptor learning phase utilizes a training set of synthetic images rendered from 3D models, while the pose optimization stage operates on a pre-existing 3D surfel map. Experiments conducted on the 7-Scene and 7-View datasets demonstrate that this strategy achieves superior relocalization performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

The rapid proliferation of mobile devices has fueled significant interest in privacy-preserving machine learning, particularly federated learning (FL). FL allows a central server to train a global model by aggregating updates from distributed clients, thereby avoiding the exposure of sensitive local data. However, FL faces the challenge of heterogeneity, where data distributions vary significantly across clients, potentially compromising model performance. Additionally, in many practical scenarios, obtaining extensive labeled datasets on each client is infeasible, necessitating the use of semi-supervised learning (SSL) to leverage unlabeled data. To address these dual challenges of heterogeneity and data scarcity, this study introduces a novel ambiguity minimization-based SSL framework tailored for personalized federated learning. By jointly optimizing ambiguity minimization and knowledge distillation, the proposed method effectively mitigates client-side data bias and facilitates the transfer of robust knowledge from the global model to individual clients. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques across various benchmarks.

Black hole–neutron star (BH-NS) mergers are a primary source of heavy r-process elements and neutrinos, which are essential for synthesizing these elements. In this study, we conducted a series of 3D general-relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations incorporating neutrino radiation, focusing on BH-NS mergers that result in the formation of a black hole. Our work examines how varying initial magnetic field strengths, configurations, and the neutron star's equation of state influence the post-merger dynamics and the subsequent emission of neutrinos. We analyzed the evolution of the remnant object, the production of r-process elements, and the neutrino spectra. Our results indicate that the post-merger phase is highly sensitive to these initial conditions. Specifically, stronger magnetic fields and stiffer equations of state lead to more extended neutron star remnants and significantly boost the production of r-process elements. Additionally, the neutrino spectra are markedly affected by these parameters, with stronger magnetic fields and stiffer equations of state generally resulting in lower average energies.

This paper introduces a twisted version of the regular genus for a compact Riemann surface, defined via an associated twisted determinant line bundle. We establish a Riemann surface analogue of the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem to prove that the twisted regular genus remains constant. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for this quantity and examine its application to the moduli space of such surfaces.

The Q-function serves as a cornerstone in reinforcement learning, yet its convergence properties have remained largely unexamined. This study introduces a novel class of problems termed "uniformly solvable Markov decision processes" (MDPs), for which the optimal Q-function converges to the true optimality. We demonstrate that within this framework, both asynchronous and synchronous Q-learning algorithms converge uniformly to the optimal Q-function. Furthermore, for MDPs exhibiting a uniform mixing property, the rate of this convergence is explicitly established.

This study investigates the optical binding of nanoparticles within a graphene substrate, driven by surface plasmons in the terahertz frequency range. We demonstrate that graphene's tunable optical properties enable precise control over optical forces acting on the particles. Specifically, we show that adjusting the Fermi energy allows for the manipulation of both the magnitude and direction of these forces, facilitating either attraction or repulsion between them.

This study investigates the impact of varying treatment durations in the Emergency Department (ED) on the average time spent in the system, utilizing a queuing framework. The analysis demonstrates that reaction curves, representing the average ED residence time as a function of treatment duration, are unimodal. Furthermore, the study derives the optimal treatment duration that minimizes total system time for various scenarios.

This study investigates the synchronization of a distributed system of robots, where each agent executes multiple tasks and must align its execution with those of others. The system's dynamics are modeled as a linear time-invariant framework, where agents exchange state information through a time-varying network. The primary objective is to develop distributed protocols that achieve synchronization for all robot agents. The proposed method integrates a communication strategy with a local computation plan, ensuring that the synchronization process aligns with a predefined schedule. The paper presents the design of such a protocol and proves that synchronization is guaranteed when the alignment schedule corresponds to a common periodic graph sequence. The findings are supported by numerical simulations.

The LHC's heavy-ion collisions generate intense magnetic fields alongside substantial vorticities, potentially driving chiral charge separation via the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME). This phenomenon predicts that like-charge pairs will exhibit enhanced production perpendicular to the reaction plane, an effect expected to be more pronounced in unlike-charge pairs. To investigate CME, the ALICE collaboration analyzed charge-dependent azimuthal correlations in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ of 2.76 and 5.02 TeV, comparing results from central and semi-central events. The study measured the difference in the two-particle correlation strength between same-sign and opposite-sign pairs, normalized by the event plane angle, alongside the three-particle correlation involving the event plane. The observed excess of same-sign correlations is notably lower than that seen in unlike-charge pairs, aligning with CME predictions. Furthermore, the data exhibit a dependence on the reaction plane orientation, consistent with expectations from the CME.

The surge in online fundraising platforms has enabled individuals to gather funds for a diverse array of causes, ranging from medical expenses and disaster relief to charitable donations. This study examines the signals within the crowd that correlate with successful campaigns, utilizing data from three distinct platforms: GoFundMe, Kickstarter, and Indiegogo. The analysis focuses on both textual and structural elements, including the campaign narrative, creator's profile, and network connections. The findings indicate that textual elements exert a more significant influence on fundraising success than structural factors. Furthermore, the study reveals that the impact of these signals varies across different platforms.

The rapid evolution of cyber threats necessitates that organizations continuously update their intrusion detection systems (IDS) with the latest threat data. However, privacy concerns and the high costs associated with acquiring such data often hinder organizations from effectively combating emerging threats. This study introduces a novel threat intelligence sharing framework leveraging federated learning to train a unified IDS across multiple entities while preserving local data privacy. The system employs a dynamic, adaptive mechanism to adjust the learning contributions of each organization based on their specific threat data characteristics. Additionally, it incorporates a mechanism to identify and exclude malicious participants attempting to undermine the global model. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach outperforms traditional methods, delivering superior detection accuracy while maintaining data confidentiality.

Multi-point robotic manipulation involves a single robot arm visiting multiple locations to perform tasks like placing or picking objects. This study addresses the challenge of determining the most efficient visit sequence for a given set of object locations. We introduce a novel greedy algorithm that leverages geometric grouping to solve this problem. The method begins by clustering task sites based on their spatial geometry and then constructs the path by iteratively visiting these clusters. We provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that this approach is bounded by a constant factor relative to the optimal solution. Additionally, we present an efficient implementation of the algorithm and evaluate its performance through simulations and physical experiments.

High-mobility Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) technology has emerged as a leading candidate for future nanoelectronic systems, offering distinct advantages over bulk silicon. This study details the fabrication of SOI devices using a 300 mm full CMOS manufacturing line, achieving hole mobilities of 120 cm²/Vs and electron mobilities of 800 cm²/Vs. The research examines the electrical characteristics of these high-mobility devices, including their transport mechanisms and threshold voltage shifts, and compares these findings with standard bulk CMOS devices.

This study investigates the dynamics of a two-group system where individuals within each group interact through local consensus mechanisms. We demonstrate that stable equilibria exist for two types of global interaction patterns: one where groups are completely isolated, and another where they are fully interconnected. For the isolated scenario, we establish the existence of equilibria featuring group-specific parameter mismatches, meaning the two groups settle on distinct values. In contrast, when groups are fully linked, a unique equilibrium emerges where both groups share identical parameters. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of these states and prove that group harmony is maintained in the isolated case. However, if the system is perturbed by noise, the lack of stability in the parameter-mismatched equilibrium causes the groups to converge toward a state of harmony.

Video retrieval systems frequently suffer from a bias toward popular content, which often overlooks niche or specialized videos. This study introduces a novel virtual agent framework designed to audit video search result diversity. The proposed system employs multiple agents with distinct profiles to simulate user queries, thereby assessing diversity across various domains. Additionally, the work presents a new metric for quantifying diversity within the video retrieval context. Experimental results using the MSR-Videor dataset confirm that the current state-of-the-art video retrieval model exhibits a significant preference for specific domains.

We examine monodromy defects within the Wess-Zumino model in two dimensions, which serves as an effective description of the second-order phase transition occurring in the Ising model. By applying bootstrap techniques, we derive constraints on the scaling dimensions of relevant operators and the anomalous dimensions of the monodromy defect itself. Our analysis indicates that the standard assumption of $Z_2$ symmetry, often employed in such models, is unnecessary for establishing these bounds.

We introduce a novel family of elliptic curves defined over cyclic cubic fields that possess a rational point with rank 13. This family is built upon the modular curves $X_0(11)$ and $X_0(11) \times X_0(11)$, utilizing specific genus 2 Jacobians. We provide strong evidence indicating that the curves in this family achieve the maximal possible rank for their respective fields.

This study investigates a medium access control (MAC) framework for wireless networks where interference is a dominant factor. In this model, each node independently selects a transmission rate from a predefined set and a corresponding power level, with the goal of maximizing its own throughput. The authors establish the existence of a Nash equilibrium within this system and prove that such an equilibrium can be reached through fully distributed, asynchronous updates. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that these update rules are straightforward to implement at each node on a local basis.

In graph classification tasks, auxiliary node features are often employed to enhance performance. However, when these features are irrelevant or noisy, they can hinder model accuracy. We introduce a method for automatically generating pseudo-auxiliary nodes using a self-supervised approach, which has been validated on data with up to 99% label noise. Our findings indicate that this technique improves Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) performance, particularly in scenarios with scarce labels.

Video processing is a computationally demanding task, and many algorithms are further hindered by inefficient short-range pattern matching. This paper introduces a novel approach called PatchNet, designed to handle such matching tasks with high speed and precision. The method leverages a lightweight convolutional neural network to identify and match image patches. We demonstrate that the network's architecture can be automatically derived from a specific loss function, allowing for the end-to-end training of the system using only a few examples. Additionally, we present a new loss function specifically tailored for this architecture. Extensive testing on various video processing applications confirms that PatchNet achieves both superior accuracy and significant computational speedups.

This study investigates the multi-point statistical distributions for discrete cyclic time Totally Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Processes (TASEP) on a ring, where particles enter and exit at specific sites. We derive a closed-form expression for the two-point correlation at two distinct nodes and propose a computationally feasible method to calculate these statistics for any number of points. Furthermore, we analyze the large-system limits, demonstrating that the two-point distribution converges to a Bessel process.

This study investigates the optimal allocation of transmit resources in a dual-functional wireless network designed to support both information transfer and simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) for energy-constrained devices. The architecture comprises a single access point (AP) and a set of users, each assigned a specific data service and an associated energy harvesting rate. The optimization framework aims to minimize total AP transmit power by adjusting the users' power-splitting ratios and time-division duplexing (TDD) frame durations. The resulting non-convex optimization problem is resolved through an iterative algorithm that employs successive convex approximation (SCA) to achieve convergence to a local optimum. Furthermore, the paper introduces a suboptimal, low-complexity solution based on Lagrangian duality. Simulation results validate the proposed methods and illustrate the impact of various parameters on network performance.

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of an interacting SU(N) symmetric Fermi gas, employing a variational approach grounded in the Gaussian ansatz to derive both exact results and controlled approximations. Our analysis covers the entire spectrum of interaction strengths, spanning from the unitary limit to the regime of weak repulsion. Specifically, we examine how thermodynamic variables vary with temperature and density, while also analyzing the equation of state and the speed of sound. Our findings reveal that, in the low-temperature limit, the equation of state aligns with that of a non-interacting SU(N) symmetric gas.

This study introduces an electrical circuit model for a specific type of microwave optomechanical system, where a transmission line resonator couples to a superconducting piezoelectric mechanical oscillator. We demonstrate that this system's behavior can be mapped to a parallel RLC circuit featuring a variable capacitance. This variable aspect arises from the displacement of the superconducting oscillator's center-of-mass mode, which influences the resonator's electromagnetic field via the position-dependent boundary conditions. Consequently, the system's dynamics are governed by the interaction between a control field and the resonator, creating an effective coupling between the RLC components. We further analyze the system's nonlinearity and its capacity for quantum state manipulation, including the generation of squeezed states.

This paper introduces a class of orthogonal polynomials featuring a generalized Airy-type weight function. We derive the associated recurrence relation and establish several properties of the resulting generalized Airy orthogonal polynomials.

This study examines the phase transitions occurring in wall-following robots, a classic example of disordered systems. We analyze both random environments and those featuring periodic structures, demonstrating that the robot's behavior can be modeled as a random walk on a graph. By applying renormalization group techniques, we identify the critical exponents associated with the robot's dynamics. Furthermore, we derive a new class of disordered systems characterized by a non-compact spin variable, which allows for the calculation of the robot's average localization length.
This work extends the results found in arXiv:2009.00933 to the case of chiral fermions on a two-dimensional orientable globally hyperbolic spacetime.

Laparoscopic surgery is susceptible to image degradation caused by smoke, which can obscure the surgical field and hinder the surgeon's visibility. To mitigate this, a deep learning-based system was developed to detect smoke and automatically trigger the smoke evacuation fan. However, the study reveals that applying image enhancement techniques does not necessarily improve the detection of smoke images.

The Mølmer–Sørensen gate stands as a vital tool for generating two-qubit entanglement in trapped-ion quantum computers, relying on the collective motion of ions coupled with bichromatic laser fields. However, the gate's fidelity is compromised by the fact that different motional modes contribute unevenly to the operation, a flaw exacerbated by mode frequency detuning. This study introduces a strategy to achieve balanced contributions from all motional modes by precisely engineering the waveform of the applied control signals. We demonstrate that this approach significantly enhances the fidelity of the gate, particularly in systems with a large number of ions.

The structural characteristics of ferroelectric and relaxor perovskites are defined by the displacement of atoms from their ideal positions, a phenomenon that can be visualized as the interaction between an ideal lattice and point defects. This study introduces a methodology to generate microscopic images of such systems by utilizing the concept of structural prototypes. We apply this approach to BaTiO$_3$, a classic ferroelectric, and to the relaxors Pb(Zr,Ti)O$_3$ and (Ba$_{0.7}$Ca$_{0.3}$)TiO$_3$. In these materials, the structural motifs consist of the ideal perovskite unit cell modified by the localized presence of oxygen vacancies or Sr defects. Our findings indicate that these images reveal distinct local ordering patterns within the structural prototypes, offering a new perspective on the atomic-level organization in these complex oxides.

This study introduces a unified framework linking graphical multivariate Gaussian processes (GMPs) and functional Gaussian graphical models (FGMMs). In a GMP, the covariance structure is defined by a kernel function, whereas an FGMM models the covariance between functional variables using a functional Gaussian model (FGM). We demonstrate that these two approaches are mathematically equivalent, with the FGM serving as the kernel's covariance. Furthermore, we outline a methodology for constructing FGMMs by employing existing FGMs.

Quantum computing relies on unitary transformations, which are mathematically represented by quantum circuits. However, the physical implementation of these circuits is often hindered by limited qubit connectivity, requiring additional gates to overcome connectivity constraints. These extra operations increase circuit depth, which can negate the benefits of quantum speedups. To address this, we introduce deterministic methods for optimizing circuit depth by compiling circuits that exhibit recurrent patterns. Our approach specifically targets two scenarios: (1) when the recurrence period is known beforehand, and (2) when it is unknown. In both instances, our algorithms achieve a polynomial runtime. Furthermore, our methods are general enough to handle various system topologies and distinct gate sets.

This study investigates the average-case behavior of convex optimization problems featuring random constraints. We demonstrate that, on average, random feasible regions conform to their respective mathematical limits within the convex class. Specifically, for uniformly random polytopes, we establish average-case results regarding the convergence of the volume of their associated Gaussian width, as well as the Euclidean distance from the origin to the nearest point on the boundary. These findings are extended to general convex sets, where we prove average-case convergence of the log-concave density of the projection onto the set. Furthermore, we address average-case stability in the context of convex body reconstruction.

This study introduces a theoretical framework for modeling excitonic polaron spectroscopy, a technique designed to detect individual excitons within excitonic insulators. We develop a variational approach to calculate the excitation spectrum, which accounts for both collective modes and single-particle excitations. Our results indicate that excitonic polaron spectroscopy can effectively probe the excitonic insulator state in systems composed of atomically thin layers.

This study introduces a message transmission-based adaptive message passing algorithm designed to handle nonconvex positioning and tracking challenges in scenarios involving significant noise and obstacles. The method utilizes a probabilistic data association (PDA) framework to estimate the likelihood of data association, thereby mitigating the impact of false alarms and missed detections. Furthermore, the algorithm dynamically adjusts the covariance of process noise to account for unpredictable target maneuvers. Simulation outcomes demonstrate the superior performance of this proposed approach when compared to standard centralized and decentralized methods.

This study examines $W^{\pm}Z$ production in $pp$ collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector at the LHC. The analysis focuses on the polarization states of the $Z$ boson and investigates correlations between the $W$ and $Z$ polarization vectors. The observed data aligns with Standard Model predictions. Furthermore, the study measures the cross-sections for $W^{\pm}Z$ production, categorized by the polarization states of the $Z$ boson.

The tensor product of two vectors yields a rank-2 tensor, and this concept extends to any number of indices, forming what is known as a tensor fabric. This paper demonstrates that the fabric of any tensor type encapsulates all inherent information regarding that tensor. Furthermore, we establish a specific index-lowering fabric for Riemann curvature tensors capable of representing the Riemann tensor entirely. By utilizing this construct, the Einstein field equations are reformulated as a set of first-order differential equations.

This work establishes a representation theorem for orthomodular lattices by introducing a novel spatial concept termed the topological spectrum, which serves as the topological dual of a given orthomodular lattice.

This paper introduces Coq-PSV, a Coq plugin designed to render proof scripts as interactive pen-and-paper style visualizations. These graphics can be manipulated directly using a digital stylus or mouse within a touch-compatible environment.

This paper establishes a precise limit regarding the fourth moment of normalized fourth-degree holomorphic Hecke cusp forms. The proof utilizes the Kuznetsov trace formula alongside the fourth moment of Ramanujan zeta functions, with the latter derived via the Hardy-Littlewood circle method.

This study examines the convergence behavior of two prevalent linear system solvers within the framework of Interior Point Methods (IPMs) for solving linear programming (LP) issues. We introduce a novel stopping criterion specifically for these solvers, demonstrating that it guarantees the IPM's global convergence. Furthermore, we present a new criterion tailored for the Conjugate Gradient (CG) solver, proving its ability to ensure global convergence as well.

Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly integrated into critical sectors like healthcare and transportation, where errors can lead to severe consequences. Although the field has seen significant progress, AI systems remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs that cause malfunctions. This paper introduces the AI Incident Database, a novel resource designed to mitigate future real-world AI failures by documenting past incidents. This database offers a structured, searchable collection of reported accidents, including details on the application domain, the specific nature of the incident, and the underlying causes. By enabling researchers to track the frequency of problems across various AI domains, the database supports the development of more robust and dependable systems.

We introduce a gradient descent-based approach to the exact renormalization group (ERG) within the context of four-dimensional $\phi^4$ theory. This method offers a straightforward way to solve ERG flow equations across all momentum scales, yielding smooth and continuous trajectories for the effective average action. Numerical simulations demonstrate that this technique successfully captures the essential features of the Yang-Mills Yang-Mills effective average action, including its asymptotic behavior at high momenta and the identification of the Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills Yang-Mills

Process descriptions utilizing high-level formalisms offer advantages such as enhanced expressivity and the ability to leverage domain-specific features, yet they introduce the risk of conflicts that may arise during execution. This paper addresses the monitoring of Process Algebra (PA) descriptions enriched with timed automata, focusing on scenarios where such conflicts occur. We propose a monitoring approach that employs the product construction of the process model and a reference automaton designed to accept only conflict-free execution traces. This solution is demonstrated to be sound and complete regarding the conflict-freeness of trace histories and is proven to maintain a finite state. Furthermore, we establish the complexity of this approach and provide an illustrative case study.

The Quipper programming framework enables the formal specification of quantum circuits and their evolution, with Proto-Quipper-M extending this capability to model the distinct characteristics of the classical-quantum hybrid environment. This paper introduces a process semantics for Proto-Quipper-M, treating its programs as interacting processes within a shared classical memory. We formally establish a correspondence between our process semantics and an existing denotational semantic model, thereby ensuring consistency. Furthermore, we outline the computational complexity associated with executing these processes.

This study examines the distribution of the maximum eigenvalue magnitude across various random matrix ensembles. We observe that the probability density function (PDF) of this statistic exhibits a scaling law near the origin, with the scaling function's shape contingent upon the specific RMT ensemble selected. Furthermore, the critical behavior at the boundary is analyzed, revealing a universal class characterized by a PDF vanishing with an exponent of $1/2$ and a mean value following a power law with exponent $1$. The paper also derives the corresponding large-$N$ effective action for this extreme statistic, which accounts for the observed universal critical dynamics.

We introduce a novel mechanism for simulating bosonic two-photon (or pair) generation and the associated squeezing effects. This protocol utilizes an ensemble of long-lived neutral atoms interacting with an optical cavity, where the atomic spin squeezing is harnessed to produce effective bosonic squeezing. The proposed system offers a versatile and adaptable framework for creating and manipulating squeezed states of light, with specific applications in enhancing the precision of optical phase measurements.

Genome assembly involves reconstructing a genome from sequencing reads, a task that has become increasingly vital for analyzing long-read data. This study introduces a new method for creating contigs from long reads, designed specifically to leverage the capabilities of distributed-memory parallel systems. The approach utilizes a distributed suffix trie to efficiently identify matching regions between pairs of reads. By parallelizing the contig generation process, the method significantly accelerates the overall assembly workflow. Additionally, the system incorporates a memory-efficient strategy for handling the distributed suffix trie. Experimental results demonstrate that the method achieves superior performance in both speed and memory usage compared to existing state-of-the-art solutions.

This study investigates a new delayed logistic equation, which incorporates a cell biological mechanism accounting for both cellular maturation and division. We establish that the system possesses either a stable positive equilibrium or a unique positive periodic solution, depending on whether the delay is constant or variable. Additionally, global existence of solutions is proven for both the constant and time-varying delay scenarios.

Statistical depth measures the centrality of a data point within a set, offering a non-parametric approach to multivariate outlier detection and defining a robust median. For point process data, existing methods often rely on specific assumptions regarding data structure or the data's inherent geometry. This study introduces a novel, assumption-free methodology for computing the depth of point process realizations by adapting the Isotropic Log-Ratio (ILR) transform, a technique traditionally used for compositional data. This approach leverages the robust half-width width (RHW) as its central metric. Simulation results demonstrate that this new method outperforms current alternatives in outlier detection accuracy.

We introduce a novel architecture combining superconducting qubits and hybrid inductively-capacitive (LC) resonators, designed to function as an ideal quantum device for both simulation and computation. This design leverages the distinctive properties of LC circuits, which support a vast spectrum of highly excited quantum states. By coupling these circuits with qubits, the system enables the manipulation of extensive quantum many-body environments. Furthermore, the proposed structure offers a robust framework for building quantum interfaces that link diverse quantum modalities.

The Skyrme energy density functional is employed to investigate the ground-state characteristics of Ge isotopes spanning mass numbers A = 60 to 76. This study examines the evolution of nuclear radii, single-particle energy levels, and the deformation of the nuclear shape. Furthermore, the deformation-driving mechanisms within this mass region are analyzed.

This study introduces a new method for determining the masses of short-lived nuclei by utilizing the $B\rho$ value of the magnetic field within a Penning trap. The technique relies on measuring the cyclotron frequency of ions, which is directly proportional to the $B\rho$ value, alongside a precisely calibrated magnetic field. This novel approach was employed to conduct high-precision mass measurements on the isotopes $^{100}$Rf, $^{101}$Rf, $^{102}$Rf, $^{102}$Sg, $^{103}$Sg, and $^{104}$Sg. The experimental results yielded the first-ever mass data for $^{100}$Rf, $^{101}$Rf, $^{102}$Sg, and $^{104}$Sg, while providing the most precise measurements to date for $^{102}$Rf and $^{103}$Sg. Furthermore, the derived nuclear binding energies and nuclear deformation parameters were calculated, with the resulting binding energy systematics analyzed to offer insights into nuclear deformation trends.

We introduce a novel framework for continuous lattice regularization, grounded in the Stochastic Quantization equations. This approach maintains renormalization group invariance by dynamically adjusting the bare mass alongside other bare parameters. We propose a new class of flow equations driven by the Stochastic Quantization process, which continuously evolves the coupling constants from their bare values toward the physical continuum limit. This method offers a systematic procedure for solving these flows, enabling the computation of coupling constants directly from lattice correlation functions.

We introduce a new approach to structured text recognition that integrates the syntactic regularities inherent in such data. Our method employs a biasing technique that leverages regular expression constraints to refine the outputs of an existing end-to-end text recognition model. Specifically, we demonstrate how this strategy can be applied to identify and extract tables from documents. Experiments conducted on the ICDAR 2013 Table VQA dataset indicate that our method substantially improves the performance of established state-of-the-art models.

This study investigates the generation of top quarks in proton-nucleus (pA) and nucleus-nucleus (AA) collisions at the LHC, utilizing the POWHEG+PYTHIA8 framework. The analysis focuses on the differential cross-sections for $t\bar{t}$ production as a function of transverse momentum ($p_T$) and rapidity ($y$), alongside the ratio of nuclear to proton-nucleus cross-sections ($R_{pA}$) and nuclear modification factors ($R_{AA}$). The results indicate that the $p_T$ and rapidity distributions for $t\bar{t}$ in pA collisions exhibit significant enhancements relative to pp collisions, with the magnitude of this enhancement depending on the specific nuclear species involved. In contrast, the $R_{AA}$ distribution for $t\bar{t}$ in AA collisions displays a suppression pattern, particularly at high transverse momenta. These findings suggest that top quark production in pA and AA interactions can serve as a valuable probe for investigating the properties of the nuclear medium.

Current state-of-the-art text-to-SQL models are typically trained on domain-specific datasets, which limits their ability to generalize to unseen domains. While few-shot approaches have been proposed to address this, they often fail to perform adequately when the target domain contains a large number of unique terms. To overcome these challenges, this paper introduces a novel auxiliary task designed to facilitate zero-shot generalization across domains. By leveraging the strong correlation between natural language queries and SQL statements, the model learns to generate queries that mirror the structure of the target SQL, thereby enhancing its ability to interpret natural language inputs. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing few-shot and zero-shot methods.

The LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) is a low-frequency radio project designed to map the sky, with the first data release (DR1) covering a 400 square degree area. This survey targets the sky region between declinations of -2° and +2°, spanning right ascensions from 0h to 8h. This study examines the LoTSS DR1 catalogue, which includes 1,000,000 sources brighter than a flux density of 0.25 mJy. We investigate the power spectrum and galaxy bias of these sources, utilizing a sample of 1,000,000 objects with S/N > 5. The analysis reveals a power spectrum that aligns with predictions from the Lambda Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) model, showing a slope of -2.75 at k = 0.01 h Mpc⁻¹. Additionally, we identify a significant correlation between the source distribution and the large-scale structure of the universe, indicating a bias factor of 1.5.

High-dimensional linear regression with rank constraints is a critical yet difficult issue in data science. This paper introduces a novel, efficient algorithm for resolving high-rank Lasso issues, grounded in a new adaptive sieving technique. We establish the convergence of this method and prove its finite convergence to a global optimum, supported by rigorous complexity analysis. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed approach achieves superior performance in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness compared to existing methods.

We establish a universal lower limit on entropy production during arbitrary finite-time transitions of arbitrary quantum systems, governed by the rate of change in system parameters. This bound holds even for rapid and minimal-dissipation quantum drives. Our findings are illustrated through applications to two cases: the sudden quench of a two-level system and the acceleration of a quantum harmonic oscillator.

Although AI-driven tools are increasingly deployed to address environmental challenges, their inherent ecological footprints remain largely unexamined. This study introduces a framework for assessing AI systems by integrating the carbon emissions associated with their training and deployment phases. Applied to a suite of environmental AI models, the analysis reveals that the carbon footprint of these solutions is predominantly driven by the training process. Furthermore, the research uncovers a counterintuitive phenomenon: as the accuracy of an AI model improves, its total carbon emissions rise, with the training phase accounting for the vast majority of these costs.

Prescriptive procedure monitoring aims to suggest optimal adjustments to current workflows based on observed data. While the field has seen significant advancements in recent years, many existing approaches remain constrained by rigid assumptions regarding workflow structures, resource capabilities, or the specific nature of activity transitions. This paper reviews the current state of prescriptive procedure monitoring, identifies prevailing limitations, and proposes avenues for future research to advance the domain.

This study introduces a multigoal-focused framework for controlling the thermal processing of materials, utilizing an extended Boussinesq model that accounts for both conductive heat transfer and convective effects driven by thermal expansion. The approach defines two primary objectives: a multigoal-postprocessing step evaluates the outcomes of a prior heat treatment against specific criteria, while a multigoal-a priori stage determines the optimal control parameters to best achieve those goals. To ensure computational efficiency, an adaptive finite element method is employed, featuring a novel $H^1$-based a posteriori error estimator. Numerical simulations demonstrate the efficacy of this strategy within the context of annealing steel.

The Stacking problem, defined on a directed acyclic graph (DAG), involves assigning a value to each node such that the absolute difference between connected nodes is minimized while satisfying specific node constraints. This problem has applications in fields like chip manufacturing and 3D printing. We introduce a new kernelization technique for Stacking that achieves a size reduction to $O(k^2)$ in $2^{O(k)}$ time, where $k$ represents the sum of the problem's parameters. This approach improves upon the previously known kernel size of $O(2^k k^2)$ proposed by Bredereck et al. (2019).

This study investigates the interplay between opinion dynamics and social network structure, specifically focusing on how attitudes evolve when individuals are aware of their neighbors' identities. We introduce a model based on preferential flipping, where a person's stance changes only if a majority of known contacts hold the opposing view. This mechanism operates within a system featuring two opposing camps and incorporates both direct and indirect influence. Our analysis reveals that global opinion stability hinges on the interplay between initial conditions and network topology. We demonstrate that when a significant portion of the population initially holds one attitude, confidence in that camp remains high, even if the network structure shifts toward structural balance. Conversely, if the initial distribution is nearly even, confidence in both camps declines as the network approaches a balanced state.

We investigate the internal structure of a specific class of black holes, defined by asymptotically flat exteriors and surface-boundary hair. This boundary hair arises from a scalar field that condenses on the event horizon, a phenomenon resulting from the interplay between the field and gravity within a non-minimal framework. Our analysis reveals that the resulting stellar interior consists of a fluid exhibiting negative pressure and a non-uniform density. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the matter within the core violates the dominant energy condition.

Although the timing of gene expression is vital for cellular function, the specific mechanisms governing it remain elusive. This study introduces a genome-wide modeling framework that simulates transcription dynamics by integrating experimental data on the rates of RNA polymerase (RNAP) initiation, elongation, and termination. By comparing model outputs against RNA-seq data, we discovered that transcription delays are widespread and often exceed the time required for a single RNAP to traverse a gene. Furthermore, the study identifies a strong correlation between these delays and the presence of DNA-binding proteins, suggesting that such proteins impede RNAP movement and generate significant delays. Finally, the authors propose that these timing variations serve as a mechanism for regulating cellular processes.

The low-lying 0+ states in 64Ni are examined using the interacting boson model (IBM) at a microscopic level. This study highlights that the energy gap between the 0+ ground state and the first excited 0+ state in 64Ni is primarily determined by the strength of the quadrupole-quadrupole monopole component of the IBM Hamiltonian.

This work examines contending descriptions of chiral gauge theories featuring $SU(N_c)$ symmetry and $N_f$ flavors, which lack supersymmetry. We analyze theories containing fermions in the fundamental and anti-fundamental representations alongside scalar content in both symmetric and antisymmetric tensor representations. By applying established large-$N_f$ techniques, we evaluate the infrared (IR) behavior of these models and identify candidate dualities, noting that several of these proposals extend or generalize existing results found in the supersymmetric domain.

This paper investigates the properties of linear complementary pairs (LCPs) involving group codes over $\mathbb{Z}_p^k$, where $p$ is a prime number. The authors establish the existence of an LCP for every group code and demonstrate that every group code possesses a self-dual LCP. Furthermore, the study presents a generalized version of the Kashiwara–Weil theorem applicable to group codes and derives the corresponding MacWilliams identity for these codes.

This paper introduces a compact function representation designed to accelerate inference in discrete graphical models. By leveraging the limited number of unique mappings from a domain to a range, our method significantly reduces storage requirements for tabulated functions and enables swift evaluation. We demonstrate that this approach yields an exponential speedup in calculating the Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimate for Markov Random Fields (MRFs) and facilitates rapid handling of various constraints within both discrete and continuous optimization frameworks. Empirical results indicate that the proposed representation is particularly effective for functions exhibiting sparsity or exhibiting a limited variety of distinct values.

This study introduces a novel asynchronous audio-visual learning framework designed to detect dropped objects. Unlike traditional methods, this approach accommodates discrepancies in timing and sensing modalities, allowing it to function effectively even when audio and visual data are not perfectly synchronized. The proposed solution employs a probabilistic model grounded in a hidden semi-Markov process, utilizing a particle filter for inference. Experimental evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that the method achieves superior performance compared to existing techniques.

We introduce a model that accounts for the microscopic origins of shear thickening in suspensions, demonstrating that it aligns with experimental findings. The framework establishes a global scaling relationship for the shear rate at which shear transitions occur, linking it to the system's microstructural parameters.

This study introduces a novel methodology for modeling hourly electricity consumption during crises, specifically when supply constraints force consumption reductions. The approach utilizes a Markov chain to represent the state of the power system and employs a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to forecast consumption levels based on these states. The research evaluates the proposed model using data from the 2003 North American blackout, comparing its performance against a standard HMM that ignores state transitions. Results indicate that the proposed method achieves superior accuracy, demonstrating enhanced capability in predicting hourly usage during periods of power shortages.

Personalization in Web search has become ubiquitous, raising concerns that users may overlook critical information because of algorithmic bias. While previous research has largely relied on self-reported data, this study investigates the extent to which personalization skews search results using a controlled, in-person experiment. Participants were tasked with answering questions via a standard Google search, with their result views recorded. The findings indicate that personalization significantly impacts the information users retrieve, with users in the personalized condition failing to locate the correct answers more frequently than those in the non-personalized group. Furthermore, analysis of query reformulations revealed that users subjected to personalized searches tended to alter their queries less often. These results underscore the necessity for researchers and practitioners to account for personalization effects when evaluating search engine performance.

Program synthesis involves creating source code automatically from high-level specifications. While recent deep learning methods have achieved success in this field, they are typically restricted to specific programming languages or problem domains. This paper introduces a new approach to generate code for basic arithmetic tasks by analyzing flowchart images. Our method employs a Graph Recognition Convolutional Neural Network (GRCNN) to detect nodes and edges within the flows, followed by a code generation module utilizing a Transformer. Experimental results indicate that this system outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.
The paper offers a concise overview of the reduction methods applied to the quasi-geostrophic climate model, specifically examining the challenges and constraints associated with each approach.

The Os-rich material produced during neutron star mergers is theorized to be the primary source of r-process elements found in the universe. The optical characteristics of this ejecta dictate the resulting kilonova's light curve, which serves as a vital tool for measuring cosmic distances. To accurately model the kilonova's evolution, we must calculate the opacity of the expanding ejecta, a task that demands precise atomic data for the dominant species. This study presents the first comprehensive atomic structure calculations for gold (Au) ions, a key component of osmium. We employed the multi-configuration Dirac-Fock method to determine energy levels and transition probabilities for Au IV, a low-ionization state of gold. Our results for Au IV are compared against available experimental data and the atomic spectra of isoelectonic osmium ions. Additionally, we computed the partition functions and line-averaged opacities for Au IV under the extreme conditions of kilonova ejecta.

Gastrointestinal (GI) regions encompass the stomach, small intestine, and large intestine. Although these areas are prone to various diseases, their diagnosis remains challenging due to the difficulty in detecting lesions. This paper introduces a deep learning-based method for automatically segmenting GI regions from CT images. The proposed approach utilizes a U-Net architecture, which is trained on a dataset of 100 CT scans annotated with GI masks. Evaluation results indicate that the method achieves a Dice coefficient of 0.89, demonstrating strong performance in accurately delineating the GI tract.

Compositional data consists of vectors where each element is non-negative, and the sum of all components equals a fixed constant. This paper examines the linear algebraic properties of the composition data space, highlighting how these characteristics influence the interpretation and analysis of such datasets.

The CORALIE/HARPS survey has identified 111 confirmed exoplanets with minimum masses ($M_{\rm min}$) less than 30 Earth masses. This study analyzes the distribution of these bodies across orbital periods ($P$) and semi-major axes ($a$), revealing a notable absence of planets with $M_{\rm min} < 10 M_{\rm \oplus}$ orbiting within 0.5 AU. This gap aligns with the "inner planet desert" previously predicted by photoevaporation and core-powered mass migration models.
